name: Tsuchinshan-ATLAS
summary: A naked-eye comet that reached magnitude ~0 in mid-October 2024. Rare bright comet from the Oort cloud. N. hemisphere observers saw it in the evening western sky after perihelion; S. hemisphere caught the morning show in late October.
notes: Best viewed in twilight. Developed a prominent anti-tail visible from mid-northern latitudes around Oct 14–20.

name: ATLAS
summary: A bright sungrazer-class comet that reached near-negative magnitudes during its mid-January 2025 perihelion. Predominantly visible from southern latitudes, with only brief northern-hemisphere views around discovery.
notes: Reached perihelion only 0.094 AU from the Sun, making it a Kreutz-group candidate. Most observers required an unobstructed western horizon.

name: Encke
summary: Short-period comet (3.3 yr) discovered in 1819. The October 2026 return will be unfavorable — the geometry places it well below the celestial equator for most of its peak brightness window, so southern-hemisphere observers get the better show.
notes: Generally not naked-eye; requires binoculars (mag 6–7 at best) and a very low eastern-horizon view from mid-southern latitudes.

name: Olbers
summary: A 69-year-period comet last visited the inner solar system in 2024. It brightened to mag ~7 around its June 2024 perihelion, remained observable in telescopes through late 2025, and is now receding.
notes: Not naked-eye; binocular target at best. Best positioned for mid-Northern observers in mid-2024.

name: Churyumov-Gerasimenko
summary: Famous as ESA’s Rosetta mission target (2014–2016). Returns to perihelion every ~6.4 yr; the 2029 apparition will be modestly bright (mag ~9) and observable from the Northern Hemisphere during winter and from both hemispheres by spring.
notes: Telescope-only. Best viewed for mid-Northern (~30–60° N) observers in late winter through spring 2029.
